title: Wind & Kites
strapline: On a blowy day the whole world is moving — so grab a ribbon, a kite, a windmill, and chase it.
intent: Wind is invisible but everywhere on a gusty day, and provision that captures it lets children investigate a force they can feel but cannot see.
Running with streamers, flying kites and holding windmills up to the gusts is glorious gross-motor exercise — sprinting, reaching, turning, balancing against the push.
Children test and reason: which things fly and which fall, why the ribbon streams that way, how to make the windmill spin faster.
The weather becomes observable and predictable — the trees are roaring today, the flag is snapping, it's a good kite day or a still one.
Working out how to launch and keep a kite up, often needing a friend, grows cooperation, patience and problem-solving.
Windy language blows in — gust, breeze, flutter, spin, soar, tug, whirl.
implementation: Choose a blowy day and take out a basket of wind-catchers — kites, ribbons on sticks, windmills, scarves, bubbles, a bit of light fabric.
Feel the wind first: which way is it blowing, what's it doing to the trees and the washing line, can you hear it?
Model the investigating talk: 'The windmill's stopped — how could we make it spin again? What if we run, or hold it higher?'
Offer real challenges — get the kite up and keep it up, make the longest streamer stream, find the windiest spot in the garden.
Bring in maths and comparison lightly — whose ribbon flies highest, count how long a bubble lasts, which windmill spins fastest.
Extend on still days: make paper windmills and fans to move the air yourselves, and notice how different that is from a real gusty morning.
key_questions: The windmill's stopped — how could we make it spin again?
Which way is the wind blowing — what's it doing to the trees?
Which things fly, and which ones fall — why?
Where is the windiest spot in the garden?
